items.title: Are Angels, Demons, and Miracles REAL? Why the Supernatural Matters
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "It's easy to be embarrassed when we should actually just lean into [it]."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Christian apologist Gavin Ortlund’s journey toward sharing the Gospel online began during a season of “angst,” uncertainty, and questions.

“I’ve actually been through two seasons like that, where I was just asking questions of, ‘How do I know for sure?'” he said. “I know Christ. I experience Him, but I have questions coming at me, and I wanna think through the answers.”

Ortlund said that, through these experiences, God gave him a real passion for other people and a heart to try to help people coping with doubt. Unfortunately, he said, too many people don’t see the church as a place where they can find help navigating doubts.

“So they just kinda keep it quiet and don’t talk about it,” he said. “So I just want to pastor people who are going through their own doubts. I long for non-Christians to come to know Christ.”

Ortlund said reasoning is a way to help people see the truth, but the Holy Spirit must lead the conversation. When it comes to apologetics tools, he said the supernatural is actually a powerful opportunity to help people see the Lord.

“I used to think that the weird parts of the Bible were a kind of liability that we needed to make up for with these more robust arguments to get people to sort of convince them to accept the weird things,” Ortlund said. “And I wouldn’t have worded it like that … but that’s how I was functioning and, I think, over time, I’ve come to see sometimes the weird parts are themselves an asset that we can lead off with.”

He continued, “And by ‘weird,’ you know, the supernatural — angels and demons, for example, God’s miraculous healing of people, … things like that.”

Rather than feel shame or remain silent on miracles and the supernatural, he encouraged people to lean in.

“It’s easy to be embarrassed when we should actually just lean into [it],” Ortlund said. “If we believe in the Scriptures, then we have to believe in a God who intervenes in history, and He heals people, and He supernaturally bestows His Holy Spirit in a way that none of us can understand.”

Seeing darkness leave a person or showcasing the power of a miracle can actually help point people to the Gospel in a palpable way. Ortlund said there’s consistency when it comes to how God acted in the Bible and how he still behaves today.

“If we believe in the Gospels, then we have to believe that Jesus has the power to heal and is willing to heal,” he said. “Think of the man who says, ‘If you are willing, you can make me clean,'” he said. “And Jesus has a heart of compassion for people. I think when people come sincerely to Christ, and they’re laying aside their pride, and they’re just asking for help, I think the heart of Christ is compassion, and He says to that person, ‘I am willing.'”

Ortlund continued, “I believe the heart of Christ has not changed. He’s still compassionate.”

items.title: Dallas Cowboys QB Dak Prescott Says God’s at Center of Team Culture: ‘That’s Who I Am’
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: "I've been through so much in my life..."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

On the heels of a win against the Houston Texans, Dallas Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott said faith is at the core of his team’s culture. He told reporters he and his teammates know “we’re all here because of God.”

Prescott, 33, said he and his fellow players are “all here to serve a greater purpose,” according to The Comeback.

The athlete credited Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer with establishing a faith-filled culture on the team.

“I’ve been through so much in my life,” said Prescott. “God’s always been the reason and, yeah, who I fall back on and my refuge, as I say. I can’t thank Him enough and never will be able to thank Him enough and just to see that transcend throughout our team, starting with our head coach, is special. It’s something that we take pride in.”

It’s clear Schottenheimer has embraced a celebration of faith on the team — both behind the scenes and in front of the cameras.

Cowboys cornerback Ameer Speed’s mother prayed over her son right before the team’s game against the Texans. In a clip of the powerful moment, Aricka Spencer is seen leaning over the railing in the stadium and placing her hand on Speed’s head as she held his hand and prayed for him.

BEAUTIFUL: #Cowboys DB Ameer Speed shared a special moment with his mom, PRAYING TO GOD together before taking the field against the #Texans. His mother leaned over the railing and placed her hand on his head as they prayed together before the game. https://t.co/edigB5PAuj

— MLFootball (@MLFootball) October 6, 2026

Prescott gave reporters a window into why he and his teammates are so open about their trust in God. He said the players are seeking to “be contagious” in their bold expressions of faith.

The motivation, he said, is about “opening your perspective up when things happen, win, lose or draw,” and asking God what His “purpose” is for wherever He’s placed you in life.

“We know what God wants us to do in our response and that’s being the best versions of ourselves, serving Him, serving others,” Prescott explained.

He continued, “We may not always have the answers for it, but we know what God wants us to do in our response, and that’s be the best versions of ourselves, serving Him, serving others and doing it with just pure love. I’m thankful for this team.”

Prescott also credited Jonathan and Dr. Tony Evans, both of whom serve as chaplains for the Dallas team.

The quarterback’s comments about his faith came after the Cowboys rallied from a double-digit deficit to emerge victorious against Houston with a final score of 34-30.

items.title: ‘We’re All Here Because of God’: Dak Prescott Says the Cowboys’ Open Faith Starts With Their Head Coach
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: Dak Prescott says the Dallas Cowboys have gotten more open about their faith this season, and it’s no accident. After Sunday’s comeback win over the Houston Texans, the quarterback agreed with that observation in his postgame press conference. He credited head coach Brian Schottenheimer.
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Dak Prescott says the Dallas Cowboys have gotten more open about their faith this season, and it’s no accident.

After Sunday’s comeback win over the Houston Texans, the quarterback agreed with that observation in his postgame press conference. He credited head coach Brian Schottenheimer.

“Credit ‘Schotty’ and his leadership and the way that he’s opened that up,” Prescott said. “That’s who he is. That’s who I am. That’s who a lot of the guys on our team are.”

He said the goal is for it to spread. “Trying to be contagious and understand we’re all here because of God and we’re all here to serve a greater purpose.”

Prescott said the chaplains are part of it. “We’ve got great chaplains in Jonathan and Dr. Evans, and so they’re helping lead that cause.”

He said the same approach applies to how the team responds to results. “We may not always have the answers for it, but we know what God wants us to do in our response, and that’s be the best versions of ourselves, serving Him, serving others and doing it with just pure love.”

The Cowboys beat the Texans 34-30 in Houston to improve to 2-2. They trailed 16-6 at halftime and were behind 30-27 in the fourth quarter before Prescott led a 74-yard drive in 11 plays. It ended with a touchdown pass to CeeDee Lamb with 2:15 left. KaVontae Turpin’s 48-yard kickoff return to open the second half had set up the first touchdown of the comeback.

Prescott finished 32 of 45 for 335 yards and a touchdown. Lamb caught 17 passes for 189 yards and passed Drew Pearson for fourth on the Cowboys’ all-time receiving yards list, with 7,914 career yards.

After a loss the week before, Schottenheimer’s stated goal was “find a way to finish.”

He pointed to the locker room afterward. “These guys are a special group of young men that truly do love each other,” he said. “The brotherhood is real.” He called Prescott “flawless in the second half.”

Prescott said what he’s seen on the team starting with his coach is “special.”

“I’ve been through so much in my life,” he said. “God’s always been the reason and, yeah, who I fall back on and my refuge. I can’t thank Him enough and never will be able to thank Him enough.”

Win, lose or draw, he said, the question is the same: what’s the purpose?

items.title: Recent Ratzingeria: A Scholar’s Top 10 Benedict XVI Reads
items.author: Dr. Tracey Rowland
items.summary:
Dr. Tracey Rowland

The following are the top ten publications of significant reference works that primarily deal with Ratzinger’s fundamental theology.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Tracey Rowland

The year 2027 will mark the centenary of the birth of Joseph Ratzinger and celebrations—mostly in the form of academic conferences or musical soirees—are planned throughout the world. In the Anglosphere, the celebrations will also be spurred on by the publication of significant reference works that mostly deal with Ratzinger’s fundamental theology. They include the following:

  1. Joseph Ratzinger in Dialogue with Philosophical Traditions, Vol 1: From Plato to Vattimo, and Joseph Ratzinger in Dialogue with Philosophical Traditions, Vol II: From Aristotle to Žižek, edited by Alejandro Sado, Rudy Albino de Assunção, and Tracey Rowland. (London: Bloomsbury, 2025 and 2026).

Each volume contains essays by an international team of scholars who examine Ratzinger’s engagement with over twenty different philosophers and/or philosophical traditions. Taken together, these volumes cover some forty different philosophers and traditions whose names and ideas appear in Ratzinger’s publications. These essays are invaluable for understanding the relationship between faith and reason in Ratzinger’s theology.

  1. The Inspiration and Truth of Scripture: Testing the Ratzinger Paradigm (Catholic University of America Press, 2023), by Aaron Pidel, SJ. 

This work offers a synthetic account of Ratzinger’s approach to scriptural theology in juxtaposition to three alternative approaches. The three alternatives are those of Pierre Benoit, Karl Rahner, and David Tracy. Pidel calls Benoit’s approach the Thomist-instrumental model, Rahner’s approach the Molinist-predefinitive model, Tracy’s approach the Heideggerian-disclosive model, and Ratzinger’s approach the Bonaventurian-ecclesial model. The first word in each model’s hyphenated name designates a school of thought, the second word is the way by which God becomes a true “author” of Scripture. Ratzinger’s approach comes closest to Tracy’s disclosive model, but Ratzinger and Tracy differ on the nature of the truth disclosed and the nature of the subjectivity receiving the disclosure. Heidegger’s disclosure model of truth requires one to adopt the right prejudice and thus the nature of the subject receiving the disclosure becomes very important. In Ratzinger’s thought, the Church—understood as the people of God—is the receiving subject. 
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

Fr. Pidel further argues that this approach of Ratzinger incorporates the strengths of the other three models, along with insights from St. Bonaventure, St. John Henry Newman, Romano Guardini, and Erich Przywara. 

Fr. Pidel’s book is likely to become the classical understanding of Ratzinger’s approach to scriptural exegesis and more broadly, the Scripture and tradition relationship.

  1. The much-awaited The Joseph Ratzinger Compendium (Ignatius Press, autumn 2026). 

This is a collection of 104 essays written by seventy-two scholars. Each essay addresses one topic in the theology of Ratzinger. The essays are approximately 4,000 words in length and supported with a bibliography. The first edition of the Compendium will be in English, and there are plans for editions in Spanish, German, and Italian. The chief editor is Dr. Rudy Albino de Assunção from Brazil. The late Pope Benedict was made aware of this forthcoming publication before his death, and at the time, he joked about there being seventy-two scholars to summarise his works and seventy-two scholars to translate the Hebrew Pentateuch into Greek. He was amused by this fact that had never occurred to the editors.

  1. The Oxford Handbook of Joseph Ratzinger, edited by Tracey Rowland and Francesca Aran Murphy (2026).

The Oxford Handbook of Joseph Ratzinger was published in January 2026. It contains twenty-nine essays from an international cohort of scholars. It includes contributions by theologians who worked with Ratzinger during his days as prefect for the Congregation of the Doctrine of the Faith (Don Damiano Marzotto and Don Livio Melina); an essay by Fr. Aaron Pidel on Ratzinger’s understanding of the relationship between the Petrine Office and the Episcopacy, and an essay by Fr. Vincent L. Strand, SJ, on Ratzinger’s theology of priesthood. There are also contributions from two of the leading Ratzinger scholars from Africa: Fr. Maurice Agbaw-Ebai on “Ratzinger and the Johannine Concept of Logos” and Fr. Martin Ifeanyi Onuoha on “The Mariology of Joseph Ratzinger.” The 2024 Ratzinger Prize winner Cyril O’Regan contributed a chapter on Ratzinger’s Principles of Fundamental Theology and Fr. Emery de Gaál addressed the document Dominus Iesus. These are just some of the highlights of this collection.

  1. The Cambridge Companion to Joseph Ratzinger (Cambridge University Press, 2024), edited by Daniel Cardó and Uwe Michael Lang.

The fact that both Oxford and Cambridge University Presses have published handbooks or companions to the thought of Ratzinger speaks volumes about the late pontiff’s standing in the world of theology. There is so much that can be said that the two volumes are not, for the most part, ploughing the same fields and can be read as companions to each other. The Cambridge Companion offers twenty-one essays, including contributions from such luminaries as Bishop Rudolf Voderholzer whom Benedict XVI appointed to the See of Regensburg, Thomas Joseph White, OP, the Rector Magnificus of the Angelicum, Kurt Cardinal Koch, and Fr. Thomas Weinandy, OFM Cap.

  1. The Bloomsbury series T&T Clark Studies in Ressourcement Catholic Theology and Culture has published several works about Ratzinger.
Magnificent Humanity
Get Pope Leo’s Encyclical

Fr. Gregory Morgan’s Natural Law & the Secular Mythos (2025) will resonate well with people who share Ratzinger’s approach to the faith and reason, and nature and grace relationships. David Collit’s Hope and History: The Communio and Concilium Alternatives (2026) juxtaposes approaches to the theology of history found in the works of Josef Pieper and Joseph Ratzinger and those found in the theology of Johann Baptist Metz and Walter Kasper. Isabel Troconis’s Ontological and Historical Dimensions of Salvation According to Joseph Ratzinger (2025) examines the history and ontology relationship in the theological anthropology of Ratzinger, while Tomasz Dekert’s Liturgical Peace, Liturgical War: Benedict XVI’s Summorum Pontificum and Its Critics (2025) is focused on Ratzinger’s liturgical theology.

  1. John Henry Newman and Joseph Ratzinger: A Theological Encounter (Washington DC: Catholic University of America Press, 2025). 

This is a collection of conference papers edited by Matthew Levering and Emery de Gaál. Each of the chapters showcases the intellectual affinities between Ratzinger and Newman. A similar collection on Ratzinger and Rahner showcasing the dissimilarities, collated by the same editors, will be published late 2026 or early 2027. 

  1. The Lord Holds Us by the Hand: Private Homilies, Seasons and Feasts (Ignatius Press, 2026).

This is a collection of homilies delivered by Pope Benedict XVI in private chapels and have not, therefore, been in the public domain before this publication.

  1. Beyond the Crisis in the Church: The Pontificate of Benedict XVI (St. Augustine’s Press, 2024) by Roberto Regoli.

Roberto Regoli is the director of the Department of Church History and professor at the Pontifical Gregorian University and president of the Ratzinger Foundation. This work is not an exposition of Ratzinger’s theological teaching but a history of his papacy. It offers a deep-dive into the goings-on inside the Curia during the papacy of Benedict XVI. Significant observations include the intellectual affinity of Ratzinger and Newman and the role of Tarcisio Bertone, the Secretary of State, in the politics of the era.

  1. The Mind of Benedict XVI: A Theology of Communion by Richard G. DeClue, Jr. (Word on Fire, 2024).

Richard DeClue offers a presentation of themes in the fundamental theology of Ratzinger, such as his account of the Trinity, Christology, revelation, and creation in such a way that the coherence of Ratzinger’s theological building-blocks shines forth. The concept of Communion is central to this coherence.

Finally, in addition to this top-ten list, when it comes to identifying circles of interest in Ratzinger studies, the countries of Central Europe have produced prominent scholars of Ratzinger’s thought.The Collected Works of Ratzinger have been published in Polish under the direction of Fr. Krzysztof Góźdź, who is a professor of dogmatic theology at the Catholic University of Lublin (KUL). Tibor Görföl from the University of Pécs has started the work of the translation of the Collected Works into Hungarian, and Alin Tat, a Greek Catholic theologian in the city of Cluj-Napoca (formerly Kolozsvár) in Romania, has translated numerous articles by and about Ratzinger into Romanian.

items.title: Thursday, October 8, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, our Gospel offers a wonderful promise of answered prayer: “And I tell you, ask and you will receive; seek and you will find; knock and the door will be opened to you.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Galatians 3:1-5

You foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? It was before your eyes that Jesus Christ was publicly exhibited as crucified! The only thing I want to learn from you is this: Did you receive the Spirit by doing the works of the law or by believing what you heard? Are you so foolish? Having started with the Spirit, are you now ending with the flesh? Did you experience so much for nothing?—if it really was for nothing. Well then, does God supply you with the Spirit and work miracles among you by your doing the works of the law, or by your believing what you heard?

Psalm
Luke 1:69-70, 71-72, 73-75

He has raised up a mighty savior for us
    in the house of his servant David,
as he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets from of old,
   that we would be saved from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us.
Thus he has shown the mercy promised to our ancestors,
    and has remembered his holy covenant,
the oath that he swore to our ancestor Abraham,
    to grant us that we, being rescued from the hands of our enemies,
might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness
    before him all our days.

Gospel Reading
Luke 11:5-13

And he said to them, “Suppose one of you has a friend, and you go to him at midnight and say to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves of bread; for a friend of mine has arrived, and I have nothing to set before him.’ And he answers from within, ‘Do not bother me; the door has already been locked, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot get up and give you anything.’ I tell you, even though he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, at least because of his persistence he will get up and give him whatever he needs.

“So I say to you, Ask, and it will be given you; search, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened for you. For everyone who asks receives, and everyone who searches finds, and for everyone who knocks, the door will be opened. Is there anyone among you who, if your child asks for a fish, will give a snake instead of a fish? Or if the child asks for an egg, will give a scorpion? If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!”

Reflection

Friends, our Gospel offers a wonderful promise of answered prayer: “And I tell you, ask and you will receive; seek and you will find; knock and the door will be opened to you. For everyone who asks, receives; and the one who seeks, finds; and to the one who knocks, the door will be opened.”

Petitionary prayer is one of the most fundamental ways that we raise our minds and hearts to God. It is also the most common form of prayer in the Bible. Every major scriptural character—Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Joshua, Samuel, David, Solomon, Ezra, Nehemiah, Peter, James, Paul, and John—prays in this way; they all ask God for things. 

There is something, of course, primal and elemental about this kind of prayer: “O God, please help me! O Lord, save my child!” If we could place a net capable of catching prayers as they waft their way to heaven from hospitals and churches, we would corral millions upon millions of them. Finally, the paradigmatic prayer that Jesus taught us—the Our Father—is nothing but a series of petitions, and Jesus urged his followers, again and again, to persevere in prayer.
